# Lumiose UI

> `@lumiose/ui`: accessible, unstyled UI primitives built on native elements (`<dialog>`, popover, invoker commands, CSS anchor positioning), server-rendered without hydration. Style them with your own CSS or the optional default theme.

These docs ship in `@lumiose/ui` and match the installed version: `node_modules/@lumiose/ui/docs`.
In a project that depends on it, `lumiose docs ui` prints the index and `lumiose docs dialog` a
component's page; the Lumiose MCP server's `ui_components` tool lists every component's parts,
props, events and styling hooks. The Lumiose docs: `node_modules/lumiose/docs/llms.txt`.

<!-- source: README.md -->

# UI components

> `@lumiose/ui`: accessible, unstyled UI primitives built on native elements (`<dialog>`, popover, invoker commands, CSS anchor positioning), server-rendered without hydration. Style them with your own CSS or the optional default theme.

**Status:** in development. `@lumiose/ui` keeps its own 0.x versions, apart from the version all
other Lumiose packages share, and is not on npm yet: today it is used from this repository's
workspace. The goal for its 1.0 is parity with [Base UI](https://base-ui.com)'s components; the
table below lists them as they land.

These pages ship in the package, in `node_modules/@lumiose/ui/docs`, so they match the installed
version. For coding agents, `llms.txt` indexes them and `llms-full.txt` holds them all;
`lumiose docs ui` and `lumiose docs dialog` print them; the MCP server's `ui_components` tool lists
every component's parts, props, events and styling hooks; and `lumiose agents init` adds a UI
section to `AGENTS.md` and the `lumiose-ui` skill. Every component page has the same sections:
Anatomy, API, Example, Styling, Keyboard and focus, Without JavaScript, Browser support and Related.

## Approach

- **Native first.** A component renders the element the platform already has for the job: a
  `<dialog>` opened by an invoker command, a popover, a `<button>`. Those work in server HTML
  before any script loads, and keep the browser's own keyboard handling and focus management.
- **Custom elements only where the platform falls short.** Keyboard navigation in a menu or the
  filtering of a combobox need script: those components render a light-DOM custom element with a
  `lu-` tag (`lu-menu`, `lu-combobox`) that upgrades the server HTML in place. A page is meant to
  load only the definitions of the elements it renders, and no island runtime for them (in
  development, with those components).
- **Small scripts for native gaps.** Where a native element falls short of Base UI's behaviour, a
  small script closes the gap, such as Dialog's right-click and touch handling. The component
  still works without it; a page that renders the component loads it once, without the island
  runtime.
- **Parts.** Each component is a set of parts named as in Base UI (`Dialog.Root`,
  `Dialog.Trigger`, `Dialog.Popup`, …). Every part that renders an element takes that element's
  props (`class`, `style`, `aria-*`, events) and passes them through.
- **Signals.** A component's state is a prop and a callback: `open` with `onOpenChange`, `checked`
  with `onCheckedChange`, `value` with `onValueChange`. Pass a signal's value and write it back in
  the callback to keep both in sync, or leave both out and the element keeps its own state. Custom
  elements report changes with lowercase DOM events, like native ones: `openchange`,
  `checkedchange` and `change`.
- **Keyboard contracts.** Every component follows its WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices pattern, and
  its end-to-end tests check the keyboard paths and run axe.

This is the approach of [Timeless](https://timeless.build), ported to Lumiose.

## Styling

`@lumiose/ui` is **unstyled**: its stylesheets hold only what a component needs to work
(display, positioning and anchoring, the top layer, the CSS variables a component sets), in the
`lu.core` cascade layer. A look is opt-in: the default theme, or your own CSS.

```ts
import "@lumiose/ui/styles.css"; // what every component needs (or "@lumiose/ui/dialog.css", …)
import "@lumiose/ui/themes/default.css"; // optional: the default theme
```

Both stylesheets declare the layers `lu.core, lu.theme`, in that order. CSS outside layers always
wins over layered CSS, so your own stylesheets override the package's without specificity games.
If your app orders its own layers, put `lu` first: `@layer lu, reset, components;`.

### The default theme

`@lumiose/ui/themes/default.css` is a ready look for demos, prototypes and getting started: neutral
surfaces, a blue primary, light and dark. It styles a few classes, which you put on the parts
through their `class` prop:

| Class       | On                  | Variants                                                                |
| ----------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `lu-button` | any `<button>` part | `data-variant="primary"`, `data-variant="destructive"`                  |
| `lu-dialog` | `Dialog.Popup`      | Styles the backdrop, the title, the description and a `<footer>` inside |

Its colours and radius are custom properties with shadcn/ui's names and a `--lu-` prefix, so a
shadcn palette carries over:

| Property                                          | Used for                            |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `--lu-background`, `--lu-foreground`              | Page-level surfaces and text        |
| `--lu-card`, `--lu-card-foreground`               | Cards                               |
| `--lu-popover`, `--lu-popover-foreground`         | Dialogs, popovers, menus            |
| `--lu-primary`, `--lu-primary-foreground`         | Primary actions                     |
| `--lu-secondary`, `--lu-secondary-foreground`     | Secondary actions                   |
| `--lu-muted`, `--lu-muted-foreground`             | Subdued surfaces and text           |
| `--lu-accent`, `--lu-accent-foreground`           | Hover and highlighted items         |
| `--lu-destructive`, `--lu-destructive-foreground` | Destructive actions                 |
| `--lu-border`, `--lu-input`, `--lu-ring`          | Borders, field borders, focus rings |
| `--lu-radius`                                     | Corner radius                       |

The theme sets `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root` and every colour with `light-dark()`, so it
follows the system. Set `color-scheme: light` (or `dark`) on `:root` or on any element to force
one, and redefine a property outside layers to change it:

```css
:root {
  --lu-primary: #7c3aed;
  --lu-radius: 0.375rem;
}
```

### Your own CSS

Style the parts through:

- **Class props.** Every part takes `class` (and `style`), like the element it renders. No part
  carries a class or attribute of its own.
- **State.** Components expose state the way the platform does, so selectors read it directly:
  `dialog[open]`, `:modal`, `::backdrop`, `:popover-open`, `[aria-expanded]`, `[aria-checked]`,
  `[aria-selected]`, and `data-highlighted` on the active option of a list.

Each component's page has an example stylesheet to start from.

## Components

| Component                         | Status                                                 |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| [Dialog, alert dialog](dialog.md) | Available: native `<dialog>`, works without JavaScript |
| Popover, tooltip                  | Planned                                                |
| Menu                              | Planned                                                |
| Combobox, select                  | Planned                                                |
| Tabs                              | Planned                                                |

## Size

`@lumiose/ui` is opt-in, so its size is reported apart from the runtime's caps:
`pnpm --filter @lumiose/ui size` prints, per component, the JavaScript a server-rendered page loads
for its custom elements, the JavaScript an island that uses it loads, and its CSS (minified, gzip
and brotli).

## Related

- [Web components](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/guides/web-components/): custom elements in Lumiose pages and islands.
- [Islands](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/concepts/islands/): where components run in the browser.
- [JSX](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/concepts/jsx/): `class`, events and `on:`.

<!-- source: dialog.md -->

# Dialog

> A modal dialog, or an alert dialog that needs an answer: a native `<dialog>` opened and closed by invoker commands, so it works in server HTML with no JavaScript, and a 0.8 kB script closes the native element's gaps where JavaScript runs. `bind:open` (or `open` and `onOpenChange`) keeps a signal in sync in islands.

```ts
import { Dialog } from "@lumiose/ui"; // or "@lumiose/ui/dialog"
import "@lumiose/ui/dialog.css"; // locks the page's scroll behind a modal dialog
import "@lumiose/ui/themes/default.css"; // optional: the default theme
```

## Anatomy

```tsx
<Dialog.Root>
  <Dialog.Trigger />
  <Dialog.Popup>
    <Dialog.Title />
    <Dialog.Description />
    <Dialog.Close />
  </Dialog.Popup>
</Dialog.Root>
```

| Part          | Renders                                                                                                                       |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Root`        | No element. Holds the state and the ids the other parts share.                                                                |
| `Trigger`     | `<button type="button" command="show-modal" commandfor="…" aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-expanded="…">`                         |
| `Popup`       | `<dialog closedby="…">`, labelled by its `Title` and described by its `Description`; `role="alertdialog"` for an alert dialog |
| `Title`       | `<h2>`, which names the dialog.                                                                                               |
| `Description` | `<p>`, which describes it.                                                                                                    |
| `Close`       | `<button type="button" command="close" commandfor="…">`: its `value` becomes the dialog's `returnValue`.                      |

The trigger can sit anywhere inside `Root`, and a popup may have several close buttons. `Title` and
`Description` go inside `Popup`. A dialog may contain another `Dialog.Root`: the inner dialog
opens on top of the outer one.

## API

### Dialog.Root

| Prop           | Type                        | Default    |                                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------- | --------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `open`         | `boolean`                   |            | Opens or closes the dialog when it changes, in the browser. Server HTML always starts closed: a modal dialog opens only from a trigger or script. |
| `onOpenChange` | `(open: boolean) => void`   |            | Called after the dialog opens or closes, whatever did it: the trigger, a close button, Escape, a click outside or `open`.                         |
| `bind:open`    | `Signal<boolean>`           |            | Stands in for `open` and `onOpenChange`: the signal opens and closes the dialog, and follows it.                                                  |
| `role`         | `"dialog" \| "alertdialog"` | `"dialog"` | `"alertdialog"` for a confirmation that needs an answer: a click outside does not close it.                                                       |

Without `open`, `onOpenChange` or `bind:open` the dialog keeps its own state.

### The other parts

Each part takes the props of the element it renders (`class`, `style`, `aria-*`, `data-*`, event
handlers, `ref`) and passes them through. Your props override the defaults (`type`,
`aria-haspopup`, `aria-expanded`, `closedby`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`); `id`,
`command` and `commandfor` stay the parts' own, since they connect the parts.

- **`Trigger`**: `aria-expanded` follows the dialog in the browser. In server HTML it stays
  `"false"`, which is never wrong where assistive technology can reach it: while the modal dialog
  is open, the trigger is inert.
- **`Popup`**: `closedby` is `"any"` for a dialog (Escape or a click outside closes it) and
  `"closerequest"` for an alert dialog (Escape only); pass `closedby="none"` to allow neither. Native
  events work as on a `<dialog>`: `on:close` runs after any close, and
  `event.currentTarget.returnValue` holds the value of the `Close` that closed it (it is unchanged
  after Escape).
- **`Title`** and **`Description`**: the popup's `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` point at
  the ones it renders, and only those; in an island they follow parts that appear or go away. A
  dialog without a `Title` needs an `aria-label` on `Popup`.

## Example

A confirmation in a server-rendered page, with no island, styled by the default theme:

```tsx check
import { Dialog } from "@lumiose/ui";

export function DeleteProject() {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root role="alertdialog">
      <Dialog.Trigger class="lu-button">Delete project…</Dialog.Trigger>
      <Dialog.Popup class="lu-dialog">
        <Dialog.Title>Delete project?</Dialog.Title>
        <Dialog.Description>This removes the project and its deployments.</Dialog.Description>
        <footer>
          <Dialog.Close class="lu-button" value="cancel">
            Cancel
          </Dialog.Close>
          <Dialog.Close class="lu-button" data-variant="destructive" value="delete">
            Delete
          </Dialog.Close>
        </footer>
      </Dialog.Popup>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}
```

In an island, bound to a signal: the button outside opens it, and the signal follows whatever
closes it. `bind:open={open}` is short for `open={open()}` plus
`onOpenChange={(next) => open.set(next)}`.

```tsx check
import { Dialog } from "@lumiose/ui";
import { signal } from "lumiose";

export function EditProfile() {
  const open = signal(false);
  const saved = signal("");
  return (
    <>
      <button type="button" class="lu-button" onClick={() => open.set(true)}>
        Edit profile
      </button>
      <Dialog.Root bind:open={open}>
        <Dialog.Popup
          class="lu-dialog"
          on:close={(event) => saved.set(event.currentTarget.returnValue)}
        >
          <Dialog.Title>Edit profile</Dialog.Title>
          <Dialog.Description>Your name as others see it.</Dialog.Description>
          <footer>
            <Dialog.Close class="lu-button" data-variant="primary" value="save">
              Save
            </Dialog.Close>
          </footer>
        </Dialog.Popup>
      </Dialog.Root>
      <p>{open() ? "Editing…" : `Last answer: ${saved() || "none"}`}</p>
    </>
  );
}
```

## Styling

**With the default theme**, put `lu-dialog` on `Popup` and `lu-button` on the buttons
(`data-variant="primary"` or `"destructive"` for filled ones). `lu-dialog` also styles the backdrop,
the title, the description and a `<footer>` for the buttons, and fades and zooms the dialog in and
out. Its colours come from the theme's `--lu-` properties ([UI components](README.md#the-default-theme)).

**With your own CSS**, style the parts through `class` and the dialog's native state: `dialog[open]`,
`:modal`, `::backdrop` and `[role="alertdialog"]`. Where the client script runs, a dialog with open
dialogs inside also gets `data-nested-dialog-open` and `--nested-dialogs` (how many are open inside
it), as in Base UI; `dialog:has(dialog[open])` matches the same dialogs without the script. A starting point, with a fade that keeps the dialog in the top layer while it
closes:

```css
.dialog {
  inline-size: min(28rem, 100vw - 2rem);
  padding: 1.25rem;
  border: 1px solid #d4d4d8;
  border-radius: 0.75rem;
  box-shadow: 0 10px 30px -10px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.35);
}
.dialog::backdrop {
  background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.45);
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .dialog,
  .dialog::backdrop {
    transition:
      opacity 150ms ease-out,
      overlay 150ms allow-discrete,
      display 150ms allow-discrete;
  }
  .dialog:not([open]),
  .dialog:not([open])::backdrop {
    opacity: 0;
  }
  @starting-style {
    .dialog[open],
    .dialog[open]::backdrop {
      opacity: 0;
    }
  }
}
```

`@lumiose/ui/dialog.css` holds one rule, in the `lu.core` layer: the page behind any modal
`<dialog>` does not scroll, and keeps its scrollbar's space so the layout does not shift
(`:root:has(dialog:modal) { overflow: hidden; scrollbar-gutter: stable }`). Leave the stylesheet out,
or override the rule, to let the page scroll.

## Keyboard and focus

The browser's modal dialog provides the
[WAI-ARIA dialog pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/):

| Key            | Does                                                                                                 |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Enter, Space   | On the trigger: opens the dialog.                                                                    |
| Tab, Shift+Tab | Move between the focusable elements of the dialog. The page behind is inert: focus never reaches it. |
| Escape         | Closes the dialog on top, alert dialogs included. With nested dialogs, one Escape closes one dialog. |

- **On open**, focus moves to the element with `autofocus`, or else the first focusable element
  inside, or else the dialog. Opened by touch, the dialog focuses itself instead, so no virtual
  keyboard opens over it (an `autofocus` element still gets focus).
- **On close**, focus returns to the element that had it before: the trigger, or the button that
  set the signal. If that element is gone, focus goes to another trigger of the dialog, without
  scrolling the page.
- **A click outside** closes a dialog, not an alert dialog, and only the dialog on top. A press
  that starts inside and ends outside, such as selecting text, does not count, and neither does a
  right-click or a second finger.
- Popups opened from a dialog (a menu, a select) belong inside its `Popup`: everything outside a
  modal dialog is inert.

## Without JavaScript, and the client script

The trigger, the close buttons, Escape and the click outside are HTML features: a dialog in a
server-rendered page works before any script loads, and with none. `open`, `onOpenChange`,
`bind:open` and a live `aria-expanded` need the component to run in the browser, in an island.

Where the native element falls short of Base UI's dialog, a small script closes the gap: a page
that renders a `Dialog` loads it once, as a 0.8 kB (brotli) module without the Lumiose runtime, and
islands bundle it. It covers every `<dialog>` on the page:

- a right-click or a second finger outside does not close the dialog;
- `data-nested-dialog-open` and `--nested-dialogs` on a dialog with open dialogs inside;
- a dialog opened by touch focuses itself;
- focus returns without scrolling, to the opener or, if it is gone, another trigger (WebKit, which
  does not focus a clicked button, would otherwise leave focus on the page);
- the click outside where the browser lacks `closedby` (Safari), and the invoker commands where it
  lacks them.

Until the script loads (or without JavaScript) the dialog behaves as the browser's own.

## Browser support

- **Invoker commands** (`command`, `commandfor`) open and close the dialog: Chrome and Edge 135,
  Firefox 144, Safari 26.2. In older browsers the client script stands in for them; without
  JavaScript the trigger and the close buttons do nothing there.
- **`closedby`**: Chrome 134 and Firefox 141; Safari only in Technology Preview. Elsewhere the
  client script closes the dialog on a click outside; without JavaScript only Escape does.
- **Exit animations** that keep the dialog in the top layer (`overlay`) are Chromium-only.
  Elsewhere the dialog leaves the top layer as soon as it starts closing.

  `onOpenChange`.
- [JSX](https://itsjavi.com/lumiose/docs/concepts/jsx/): native events with `on:` and `ref`.
